module.title: Analytics for Product Managers
module.subtitle: 60+ EXERCISES / 8 HOURS OF PRACTICE
module.description: Decide with data using a product-analytics system (Mixpanel-style). Insights, funnels, retention, segmentation. Case: Calmly meditation app + an online shop.

lesson.title: Reading Product Analytics Without Fooling Yourself
lesson.note: Uses the mock analytics widgets: mixpanel-insights (chart+table+grouping toggle), mixpanel-funnel (steps), mixpanel-retention (cohort grid). All fixture-driven from each tool block's config. Same grading model.

blocks.markdown: Hi! I'm the product analyst on **Calmly**. Behavioral analytics stores *everything* users do — screen views, taps, session starts. The skill isn't the tool, it's asking the right question and not fooling yourself. Let's practice.
Here's an Insights report: daily **Session Start** events for one week. Leadership asks 'how many sessions did we have Tuesday?' Read the chart.

options.label: 1,610 sessions
1,555 sessions
2,050 sessions

blocks.markdown: 1,610. Simple, but notice weekends spike — meditation happens more on days off. Always eyeball the shape, not just the one number you were asked for.
Same event, two ways to count it: **Total events** vs **Uniques**. This week Total = 11,495 but Uniques = 3,240. What does the gap tell you?

options.label: Users come back — on average ~3.5 sessions per unique user this week
Something's broken — Total should equal Uniques
We had 11,495 different users

blocks.markdown: Total counts every event; Uniques counts distinct users. 11,495 / 3,240 ≈ 3.5 sessions per user. Confusing these two is the #1 analytics mistake — 'how many people' vs 'how many times' are different questions.
We ship a new onboarding. Here's the activation **funnel**: Install → Sign up → First meditation → Set a reminder. Which step is the biggest leak to fix first?

options.label: Sign up → First meditation (45% — the steepest drop)
Install → Sign up (it's the first step)
Set a reminder (it's the last step)

blocks.markdown: Biggest leak = biggest opportunity: only 45% who sign up reach their first meditation. That's the 'aha moment' gap. Fix the steepest drop, not the first or last step by default.
Careful though — before we celebrate fixing that step, what should you check about this funnel's **time window and order**?

options.label: The conversion window (e.g. 7 days) and whether steps must happen in order — both change the numbers a lot
Nothing — a funnel is a funnel
Only the total install count matters

blocks.markdown: A funnel's numbers depend on its **conversion window** (a 1-hour vs 7-day window gives very different rates) and whether it's ordered/any-order. Always state the window when you report a funnel.
Here's a **retention** cohort grid (Week 0 = signup week, then % returning in later weeks). Two cohorts: before and after the onboarding change. What's the honest read?

options.label: The Feb cohort retains meaningfully better at every week — the change likely helped
No difference — both start at 100%
Jan is better because it has fewer users

blocks.markdown: Everyone starts at 100% by definition — read the *later* weeks. Feb holds ~23% at week 4 vs Jan's ~15%, and it's higher at every step. Retention curves are the truest measure of product-market fit; a lift that persists is real signal.
A stakeholder says 'DAU is up 20% this week, the new feature is working!' The feature launched the same week we ran a big paid-install campaign. What's the risk in that claim?

options.label: Correlation ≠ causation — the campaign could explain the DAU lift, not the feature
No risk, DAU is up so the feature works
DAU is a vanity metric so ignore it entirely

blocks.markdown: Two things changed at once, so you can't attribute the lift to the feature. To isolate it you'd need an A/B test or at least segment new-campaign users out. Confounding is everywhere in observational analytics.

Switching products: our **online shop**. Insights shows 'Add to Cart' up 15% but 'Purchase' flat. Segment tells you most of the cart lift comes from one country where a coupon leaked. What's the takeaway?

options.label: Segment before concluding — an aggregate up-trend can hide a localized, non-repeatable cause
Carts are up, so purchases will follow — ship more coupons
Purchase is flat so the shop is dead

blocks.markdown: Aggregate metrics lie by averaging. **Breakdown/segmentation** (by country, platform, cohort) reveals whether a trend is broad or driven by one slice. And carts-up-purchases-flat means the leak is downstream — check checkout.
You need a **North Star** for Calmly. Which candidate best captures delivered value (not vanity)?

options.label: Weekly users who complete ≥3 meditations
Total app downloads
Number of screens viewed

blocks.markdown: A good North Star ties to *value users actually get* and predicts retention/revenue. 'Weekly users completing ≥3 meditations' captures habit formation. Downloads and screen-views are vanity — they can rise while the product fails.
Last one. Your event tracking shows 'Purchase' fired but 'Add to Cart' didn't for 8% of buyers — impossible in the UI. Before analyzing conversion, what do you do?

options.label: Audit the tracking/instrumentation — bad event data makes every downstream metric wrong
Ignore it, 8% is small
Assume users are cheating the cart

blocks.markdown: Garbage in, garbage out. Impossible event orders signal a tracking bug (mis-fired or missing events). Data quality is a PM responsibility — validate instrumentation before trusting funnels built on it.

Excellent. You can now separate total vs unique, read funnels and retention honestly, resist correlation-causation traps, segment before concluding, pick a real North Star, and question the data itself. That's data-driven product management.
